analysis.one_liner: Doubles the number of prescription drugs Medicare must negotiate prices for, starting years earlier.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from April 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law lets Medicare negotiate prices for a limited number of expensive brand-name drugs, with the first negotiated prices taking effect in 2026. This bill would roughly double that program — 20 drugs in 2026 and 40 each year after — and would make drugs eligible for negotiation after just 3 years on the market instead of 7 (for drugs) or 11 (for biologics). It would also lower the price ceilings Medicare can't exceed in negotiations and repeal a rule barring Medicare from stepping into negotiations between drug makers and pharmacies. It died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. Millions of seniors take the brand-name drugs that would become subject to negotiation years sooner, and the federal government pays much of that bill through Medicare. Faster negotiation and lower price ceilings would mean lower out-of-pocket costs for patients and lower federal drug spending.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the Medicare negotiation program: 20 drugs in 2026 instead of 10, and 40 drugs per year from 2027 onward instead of 15, under either the drug benefit or Medicare medical services [S2][S3].

Makes drugs eligible for negotiation after 3 years of market approval instead of 7 years for small-molecule drugs and 11 years for biologics, so newer medicines reach negotiated prices far sooner [S2][S3].
Tightens the price ceilings Medicare negotiators cannot exceed — for example, the ceiling for drugs with short market exclusivity drops from 65% to 55% of the non-federal average price [S3].
Repeals the 'noninterference' rule that currently forbids Medicare from being involved in negotiations between drug manufacturers, pharmacies, and Part D plan sponsors [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose revenues would shrink as more of their top-selling drugs become subject to Medicare's negotiated maximum prices sooner, and with lower price ceilings when they are negotiated.

drawbacks.text: Faster negotiation and lower ceilings would cut revenue for drug makers, which the industry argues funds research into new medicines; an honest supporter would acknowledge that reduced expected returns could shift some investment decisions, though independent analyses of the existing negotiation program have generally projected only modest effects on the pipeline.

Doubling negotiation from day one requires CMS to build capacity quickly, and aggressive price targets could complicate negotiations — implementation risk is real, though it is an execution concern rather than a flaw in the design itself.
The bill only addresses Medicare, so Americans with private insurance would not directly benefit from these negotiated prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is lower drug prices for seniors and the federal budget versus somewhat lower revenue for brand-name drug companies, which could modestly affect investment in new drugs. The bill strengthens an existing, already-implementing program rather than creating a new one, and the main costs fall on a highly profitable industry. The strongest objection — effects on drug innovation — applies to the negotiation program generally and was already litigated when Congress created it; this bill mainly makes that program bigger and faster.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Klobuchar introduced the SMART Prices Act on April 25, 2023, with 24 original cosponsors [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day — its only action of the Congress [S5].
The bill drew 29 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, including 27 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 2 of its 4 independents [S4].
No Republican cosponsored, and with Republicans controlling the House, the bill faced long odds even if it had cleared committee [S4][S1].
The Finance Committee held no markup, and the full Senate never voted on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the faster and deeper Medicare price negotiation this bill would have required never happened. Medicare beneficiaries continue to pay the prices set under the slower, smaller existing program.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand and accelerate Medicare drug price negotiation.

for.name: 29 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including 27 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 4 independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them chaired the Finance Committee or brought it to a vote.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup was scheduled in the 20 months it sat there.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no support for the bill, leaving it with no path beyond the Democratic caucus.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug makers and their lobby
against.what_they_did: The industry has consistently campaigned against expanding Medicare negotiation, arguing it reduces revenue that funds drug development.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents — 27 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 4 independents — with no Republican support, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill makes more top-selling drugs subject to Medicare's negotiated maximum prices years earlier and lowers the ceilings those prices cannot exceed, cutting revenue on exactly the drugs where Medicare spending is highest. Its gain for ordinary people is lower prices; the industry's interest runs against that.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: Repealing the noninterference clause would let Medicare step into negotiations between manufacturers and PBMs or plans, changing a negotiation dynamic that currently excludes the government. The practical effect on PBMs is uncertain but their current protected negotiation space would shrink.
